Items 4 to 7 are every graph on three nodes, from no edges to the triangle; items 8 to 11 start the four-node graphs with zero, one, and two edges; items 15 to 18 end them with four, five, and six edges, from the paw to the complete graph." width="100%"} Returns all the graphs with up to seven nodes, up to isomorphism, in the atlas order of Read and Wilson's "An Atlas of Graphs" (1998): by number of nodes, then edges, then degree sequence, then number of automorphisms. Item `i` is the graph that `add_atlas_graph(i)` adds, built in a new undirected `Graph` whose name is `"G"`, as in NetworkX's `graph_atlas_g()`. Graph 0 is the empty graph. The atlas is useful for exhaustively checking a property or an algorithm on every small graph, and for finding the smallest counterexample to a conjecture. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The 1253 atlas graphs, in order. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} There are 1253 graphs in all, and 34 on five nodes: ::: {#abda4b10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec atlas = ec.Graph.atlas_graphs() len(atlas), sum(1 for g in atlas if g.count_nodes() == 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1253, 34) ``` ::: ::: Exhaustive checks are quick. Of the 1044 seven-node graphs, how many are planar? ::: {#4e0ab9bb .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} sevens = [g for g in atlas if g.count_nodes() == 7] len(sevens), sum(g.is_planar() for g in sevens) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1044, 822) ``` ::: ::: Each graph is named by its atlas number: ::: {#81b81c07 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} atlas[7].get_graph_name(), atlas[7].count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ('G7', 3) ``` ::: :::
